narrative:
The model predicted a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Being in the second decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaled that your later-year performance was weaker than most successful applicants. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you placed in the third decile while accepted students averaged the sixth decile. These two performance signals outweighed the third key factor—your undergraduate GPA of 3.40—which actually worked in your favor because it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students.

In short, although your college grades were solid and your family income is high, the model placed heavy weight on your relatively low law-school class standings in the first and especially the third year. Those rankings created enough concern about first-time bar passage that the admissions system could not approve the application.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance in the remaining years so that your class rank improves. Raising your standing in the program will directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction and will improve both your bar-exam prospects and future applications.
